texts.preamble: Banoth Bulli vs The State Of Telangana on 10 December, 2024 Author: P.Sam Koshy Bench: P.Sam Koshy The Hon'Ble Sri Justice P.Sam Koshy And The Hon'Ble Sri Justice Anil Kumar Jukanti Writ Petition No.33604 of 2024 Order:
texts.facts: 2. The instant is a writ petition which has been filed challenging the order dated 25.11.2024 (Annexure P-1) passed by respondent No.2 putting the detenu under preventive detention under Sub-Section (2) of Section 3 of the "The Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Bootleggers, Dacoits, Drug- Offenders, Goondas, Immoral Traffic Offenders, Land-Grabbers, Spurious Seed Offenders, Insecticide Offenders, Fertiliser Offenders, Food Adulteration Offenders, Fake Document Offenders, Scheduled Commodities Offenders, Forest Offenders, Gaming Offenders, Sexual Offenders, Explosive Substances Offenders, Arms Offenders, Cyber Crime Offenders and White Collar or Financial Offenders Act, 1986 (for short, 'the Act of 1986'). 3. The writ petition is one which has been filed seeking for issuance of a Writ in the nature of Habeas Corpus with prayer for production of the detenu before the Court and quashment of the aforementioned orders. 4. The brief facts of the case are that the detenu has been detained on 24.11.2024 in Cr.No.863 of 2024 for the offence as "BOOTLEGGER" under Section 2 (b) of Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986, in Narsampet Police Station limits. The detenu has been systematically involved in the illegal possession, purchase, transport, manufacture and distribution of I.D. (Illicitly Distilled) Liquor, in direct violation of section 7(A) read with 8(e) of the Telangana Prohibition Act, 1995 and section 34(e) of the Telangana Excise Act, 1968. The detenu's illegal activities have created a significant disturbance in public order and posed serious health risks to the local community in and around Nekkonda mandal. 5. The impugned preventive detention order is based on the four separate criminal cases registered against him at the Prohibition & Excise Station, Narsampet. These cases, bearing numbers Cr.No.123/2024 (Dated:10.03.2024), Cr.No.314/2024 (Dated: 02.05.2024), Cr.No.534/2024 (Dated: 27.06.2024) and Cr.No.863/2024 (Dated: 24.11.2024) demonstrate a pattern of repeated offenses over time. The detenu's persistence illegal activities indicate a deliberate and continuous Banoth Bulli vs The State Of Telangana on 10 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82677587/ 1 violation of the law, severely impacting the societal fabric and public health in Nekkonda mandal and its surrounding areas. 6. After careful consideration of the evidence and the nature of the offence the authorities determined that the ordinary law was insufficient to curb the detenu's unlawful activities and determined that preventive detention is necessary as a last resort. The order dated 25.11.2024, directed his detention in Central Prison, Cherlapalli, to prevent further drug-related activities that could harm public health and order.
texts.arguments: 7. Thus, the present Writ Petition challenges the impugned order on the grounds that these alleged crimes fall under the purview of ordinary law and do not constitute a disturbance of public order, questioning the necessity and legality of the detention order under the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act. 8. Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the detention order was passed based on the four cases registered against the detenu with in single year, all bearing suspicious similarities in their date of occurrence which appears to be deliberately fabricated. The learned counsel for the petitioner further contended that the detenu who earns his livelihood through manual labor has maintained a clean record with no criminal history prior to these disputed cases. He contended that it is unnecessary and improper invocation of preventive detention order when the regular criminal justice system provides adequate mechanisms to address the alleged offenses. 9. Further, the learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the detaining authority has passed the orders based on mere apprehensions rather establishing any concrete evidence or any compelling reasons to prove that the detenu is a habitual offender. However, the authority has not provided any plausible explanation for believing that the detenue would engage in activities prejudicial to public order if not detained. This absence of rational justification makes the detention order arbitrary and unsustainable in law. 10. Lastly, the detaining authorities failed to specify detention period as mandated by Section 31 of the Act which represent a serious procedural lapse. Moreover, crucial evidentiary materials including witness statements under Section 161 Cr.P.C have not been furnished with the detention order. This omission severely handicaps the detenue's ability to prepare and present an effective defense against the allegations. Thus, the learned counsel for the petitioner prayed that the impugned order of preventive detention be set-aside and the detenu be set free. 11. Per contra, the learned Special Government Pleader argued that the detenu was actively engaged in manufacturing illicitly distilled liquor through dangerous and unscientific methods and the production process was particularly concerning as it involved crude materials including black jaggery, ammonium chloride, potassium, and aluminum sulphate in disproportionate quantities. The manufacturing conditions were highly unhygienic, utilizing unclean mud pots, bamboos and rubber tubes. Laboratory analysis of the seized contraband revealed an alarming presence of harmful substances including fusel oils, acids, organic acids, higher alcohols, aldehydes, and furfural. These toxic components were found to cause severe health issues and also damage the liver Banoth Bulli vs The State Of Telangana on 10 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82677587/ 2 and nervous system. 12. Further, the learned Special Government Pleader argued that despite multiple cases being registered under the Telangana Prohibition Act, 1995, and Telangana Excise Act, 1968, the detenu showed no inclination towards reform. Instead, the detenu deliberately exploited recent amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code, particularly Section 41, which allowed release on notice. This legal loophole enabled the detenu to continue his illegal activities with impunity, creating significant challenges for law enforcement agencies. Moreover, the learned Special Government Pleader stated how the easy profits and minimal investment required in this illegal trade were encouraging the proliferation of similar offenders. The impact extended beyond immediate health concerns, as the illegal liquor trade was actively undermining government welfare schemes aimed at helping the poor and downtrodden. The detenu's activities were causing both health and financial strain on vulnerable sections of society, leading to a wider degradation of social fabric and public order. The conventional enforcement methods had proved insufficient to curb these dangerous activities, necessitating the extraordinary measure of detention under the Preventive Detention Act to effectively control and prevent further damage to society. Thus, the learned Special Government Pleader prayed for dismissal of the writ petition. 13. Having heard the contentions put forth on either side and on perusal of records, it would be relevant at this juncture to refer to a recent decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Arjun S/o. of Ratan Gaikwad vs. The State of Maharashtra 1 wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court dealing with a similar situation made a distinction between a public order and law & order and the Hon'ble Supreme Court also in the case of Ram Manohar Lohia vs. State of Bihar 2 and Ameena Begum vs. The State of Telangana 3 held in paragraph Nos.12, 13, 14 and 15 as under, viz., "12. The distinction between a public order and law andorder has been succinctly discussed by Hidayatullah, J. (as His Lordship then was) in the case of Ram Manohar Lohia (supra): "54. ...Public order if disturbed, must lead topublic disorder. Every breach of the peace does not lead to public disorder. When two drunkards quarrel and fight there is disorder but not public disorder. They can be dealt with under the powers to maintain law and order but cannot be detained on the ground that they were disturbing public order. Suppose that the two fighters were of rival communities and one of them tried to raise communal passions. The problem is still one of law and order but it raises the apprehension of public disorder. Other examples can be imagined. The contravention of law always affects order but before it can be said to affect public order, it must affect the community or the public at large. A mere disturbance of law and order leading to disorder is thus not necessarily sufficient for action under the Defence of India Act but disturbances which subvert the public order are.... . It will thus appear that just as 'public order' in the rulings of this Court (earlier cited) was said to comprehend disorders of less gravity than those affecting 'security Banoth Bulli vs The State Of Telangana on 10 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82677587/ 3 of State', 'law and order' also comprehends disorders of less gravity than those affecting 'public order'. One has to imagine three concentric circles. It is then easy to seethat an act may affect law and order but not public order just as an act may affect public order but not security of the State." 13. It has been held that when a person can be dealt with in exercise of powers to maintain the law and order, unless the acts of the proposed detainee are the ones which have the tendency of disturbing the public order a resort to preventive detention which is a harsh measure would not be permissible. 14. Recently, a Bench of this Court has referred to various judgments of this Court while following the law laid down by this Court in the case of Ram Manohar Lohia (supra), it will be appropriate to reproduce the following paragraph from the judgment of this Court in the case of Ameena Begum v. State of Telangana and Ors. "38. For an act to qualify as a disturbance to public order, the specific activity must have an impact on the broader community or the general public, evoking feelings of fear, panic, or insecurity. Not every case of a general disturbance to public tranquillity affects the public order and the question to be asked, as articulated by Hon'ble M. Hidayatullah, C.J. in Arun Ghosh v. State of W.B. [Arun Ghosh v. State of W.B., (1970) 1 SCC 98 : 1970 SCC (Cri) 67] , is this : (SCC p. 100, para 3) "3....Does it [the offending act] lead to disturbance of the current of life of the community so as to amount a disturbance of the public order or does it affect merely an individual leaving the tranquillity of the society undisturbed?" 39. In Arun Ghosh case [Arun Ghosh v. State of W.B., (1970) 1 SCC 98 : 1970 SCC (Cri) 67] , the petitioning detenu was detained by an order of a District Magistrate since he had been indulging in teasing, harassing and molesting young girls and assaults on individuals of a locality. While holding that the conduct of the petitioning detenu could be reprehensible, it was further held that it (read : the offending act) "does not add up to the situation where it may be said that the community at large was being disturbed or in other words there was a breach of public order or likelihood of a breach of public order. (ArunGhosh case [Arun Ghosh v. State of W.B., (1970) 1 SCC 98 : 1970 SCC (Cri) 67] , SCC p. 101, para 5)" 40. In the process of quashing the impugned order,the Hidayatullah, C.J. while referring to the decisionin Ram Manohar Lohia [Ram Manohar Lohia v. Stateof Bihar, 1965 SCC OnLine SC 9 : (1966) 1 SCR709] also ruled : Banoth Bulli vs The State Of Telangana on 10 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82677587/ 4 (Arun Ghosh case [ArunGhosh v. State of W.B., (1970) 1 SCC 98 : 1970 SCC(Cri) 67] , SCC pp. 99-100, para 3) "3. ... Public order was said to embrace more of the community than law and order. Public order is the even tempo of the life of the community taking the country as a whole or even a specified locality. Disturbance of public order is to be distinguished from acts directed against individuals which do not disturb the society to the extent of causing a general disturbance of public tranquillity. It is the degree of disturbance and its effect upon the life of the community in a locality which determines whether the disturbance amounts only to a breach of law and order. ... It is always a question of degree of the harm and its effect upon the community. ... This question has to be faced in every case on facts. There is no formula by which one case can be distinguished from another." 41. In Kuso Sah v. State of Bihar [KusoSah v. State of Bihar, (1974) 1 SCC 185 : 1974 SCC (Cri) 84] , Hon'ble Y.V. Chandrachud, J. (as the Chief Justice then was) speaking for the Bench held that : (SCC pp. 186-87, paras 4 & 6) "4. ... The two concepts have well defined contours, it being well-established that stray and unorganised crimes of theft and assault are not matters of public order since they do not tend to affect the even flow of public life. Infractions of law are bound in some measure to lead to disorder but every infraction of law does not necessarily result in public disorder. ... 6. ... The power to detain a person without the safeguard of a court trial is too drastic to permit a lenient construction and therefore Courts must be astute to ensure that the detaining authority does not transgress the limitations subject to which alone the power can be exercised." (emphasis supplied) 15. As to whether a case would amount to threat to the public order or as to whether it would be such which can be dealt with by the ordinary machinery in exercise of its powers of maintaining law and order would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. For example, if somebody commits a brutal murder within the four corners of a house,it will not be amounting to a threat to the public order. As against this, if a person in a public space where a number of people are present creates a ruckus by his behaviour and continues with such activities, in a manner to create a terror in the minds of the public at large, it would amount to a threat to public order. Though, in a given case there may not be even a physical attack." This Bench finds that the detaining authority has failed to make the crucial distinction between "public order" and "law and order" while passing the detention order. Further, this Bench notes that the distinction between public order and law & order is crucial in preventive detention cases. While law and order pertains to individual cases of law violations that affect specific persons, public order refers to even Banoth Bulli vs The State Of Telangana on 10 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82677587/ 5 temporary disturbances of the current life of the community in a particular area. Public order is considered to be more serious and has a larger impact on the community at large, whereas law & order situations are more localized and affect specific individuals. The Supreme Court previously has consistently held that preventive detention is an extraordinary measure that can only be justified when ordinary law is insufficient to deal with the situation. 15. Further, this Bench observes that for an act to affect public order, it must go beyond the effect on specific individuals and must disturb the even tempo of society at large. The distinction between public order and law and order lies in the degree and extent of the reach of the act in question upon society.
